Name: tokenizer_fragmentation_overthinking
Title: Fragmented Numbers, Longer Thoughts: A Tokenizer-Induced Compute Tax in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: For the identical math problem, a reasoning model spends systematically more thinking tokens when its numbers are tokenized into more fragments (worse digit segmentation), and this excess is not extra genuine reasoning but a surface-form artifact: fragmentation inflates a length/difficulty signal read at the prompt boundary before reasoning begins. Re-encoding the same numbers into fewer, cleaner tokens reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy, and the effect is causally mediated by a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation.
Related Work: Overthinking is widely studied via steerable verbosity/reflection directions (Efficiency Steering, CREST, Manifold Steering, ReflCtrl, STU-PID), uncertainty/self-doubt (ReflCtrl, Self-Doubt), neuron-based early exit (NEAT), and batch-mode resource competition (DRQA). The First Impression Problem ties overthinking to excessive attention to the input question. All treat the pre-generation length/difficulty signal as tracking genuine difficulty and study a fixed textual form. Numeral-tokenization work (Scaling Behavior of Numeral Systems; Benford's Curse) studies training efficiency and accuracy/hallucination, not inference-time compute; tokenizer non-uniqueness work (Say Anything but This) targets correctness. No prior work measures a reasoning-COMPUTE gap driven by numeral tokenization on matched problems, dissociates it from true difficulty, or locates/causally tests a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation. This is a distinct inference-time compute-allocation artifact uniting tokenizer and efficient-reasoning literatures.
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty. We show this budget is contaminated by a superficial factor: how the tokenizer segments the numbers in the prompt. Modern subword tokenizers split numerals inconsistently ('1234' as one, two, or four tokens depending on format), and we hypothesize that more fragmented numerals cause a model to think longer on the exact same problem, inflating tokens without improving accuracy. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and arithmetic-heavy word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct content-identical variants that hold the mathematical content and answer fixed while varying only numeral tokenization (native BPE, digit-spaced, comma-grouped, single-digit segmentation), verified via the tokenizer to change fragment counts. We measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per variant and test whether fragmentation predicts thinking length independent of difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition, controlling for raw prompt length. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a fragmentation-sensitive length/difficulty signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a low-fragmentation state into a high-fragmentation context and observe the budget drop), and steer it to cancel the inflation. Our work reveals a tokenizer-induced overthinking artifact and offers a simple, training-free fix (re-encoding numbers) plus a mechanistic account.
Experiments:
1) Establish the fragmentation-length effect (behavioral): For each seed math problem (GSM8K, MATH500, arithmetic-heavy word problems), generate content-identical variants changing ONLY numeral tokenization: (a) native BPE, (b) digit-spaced ('1 2 3 4'), (c) comma/underscore-grouped ('1,234'), (d) single-digit forced segmentation. Verify via the model's tokenizer that fragment counts differ while decoded text and correct answer are semantically identical. Generate reasoning traces per variant. Metrics: reasoning-token count, accuracy per variant; hypothesis: higher fragmentation -> more reasoning tokens at equal accuracy. Report within-problem effect sizes.
2) Dissociation from difficulty and prompt length: Fit a mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for problem identity (intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for fragment count and raw prompt token-length (covariate). Test the fragmentation effect after accounting for both; compare formats matched on prompt length (single-digit vs grouped vary fragmentation at similar/opposite prompt lengths) to isolate segmentation from length.
3) Rule out genuine-reasoning explanation: Use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per variant; test whether fragmentation increases WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) rather than genuine reasoning, and whether extra tokens are disproportionately re-reading/restating the numbers (lexical tagging).
4) Location - fragmentation-sensitive length probe: At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations and train a linear probe to predict reasoning length. Test whether, for identical problems, its prediction rises with fragment count. Compare to a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate); test separability via principal angles and joint-model predictive gain. Layer sweep to localize.
5) Causal intervention - patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a low-fragmentation variant into the matched high-fragmentation context (same problem) and measure whether reasoning length drops toward the low-fragmentation level. Controls: matched-random-direction patch; off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose-response, specificity.
6) Causal intervention - debiasing steering (training-free fix): Derive a fragmentation-length steering direction (difference-of-means between low- and high-fragmentation boundary states) and steer high-fragmentation prompts to cancel inflation. Compare tokens-at-equal-accuracy against no intervention, simple input-side re-encoding of numbers into fewer tokens (a deployable preprocessing fix), and fixed truncation. Metrics: accuracy, mean tokens, tokens-at-equal-accuracy, wall-clock speedup.
7) Practical payoff and generalization: Quantify, over a mixed problem stream, the tokens wasted purely due to native tokenizer fragmentation vs an oracle low-fragmentation encoding; test whether input-side digit grouping is a free efficiency win. Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether the effect is stronger for models with coarser numeral tokenization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The fragmentation effect could be an artifact of prompt token-length (digit-spacing lengthens prompts) rather than segmentation per se; the length covariate, length-matched comparisons, and single-digit-vs-grouped contrasts isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Number re-formatting could inadvertently change accuracy/difficulty; we verify answer/accuracy invariance and use tokenizer-verified content-identical variants. The fragmentation-length signal may be inseparable from a true-difficulty signal if the model genuinely finds fragmented numbers harder to parse (still a novel, actionable phenomenon but weakening the 'artifact' framing); the separability analysis and patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Effects likely depend on the model's numeral-tokenization scheme and may be small for models already using clean single-digit tokenization (an informative boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.
